opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to admit that a lot of the benchmarks we relied on stop telling you much once the paradigm shifts. When models were mainly answering single-turn questions, you could build a static test set, compute accuracy, and compare. With agents, the model is taking many steps, calling tools, recovering from its own mistakes, sometimes working for a long time. A single number at the end hides most of what matters.

So I try to look at evaluation on a few levels. One is still the outcome: did the task actually get done, in an environment that resembles real use as closely as possible? Not a simplified sandbox where the answer is basically given away, but something with real messiness: ambiguous instructions, broken tools, information that isn't where you expect it.

The second level is the process. I care a lot about reading trajectories. Honestly, some of the most valuable evaluation work is just people sitting down and reading what the agent did, step by step. You find things no metric catches: the model got the right answer by luck, or it gave up too early, or it was overconfident and never checked its work. Those qualitative observations often tell you where the next improvement should come from.

The third is that the benchmark itself has to evolve with the model. During a paradigm change, a benchmark can saturate very fast, sometimes within months. If you keep optimizing toward it, you end up overfitting to something that no longer reflects real capability. So you need to keep building harder, more realistic tasks, and be willing to throw away evaluations that have stopped discriminating.

And finally, I think you have to stay humble about what you can measure. In a transition period, a lot of intuition comes from actually using the model yourself, every day, on real work. If a model scores higher but feels worse to use, I take that seriously. Often the gap between the numbers and the experience is exactly where the paradigm is changing, and that's where the most interesting problems are.

r001.rationale: The response says intuition from daily use matters during a transition, but does not describe a brief window or condition it on the development direction being right.

r002.rationale: It recommends using the model and taking the gap between scores and experience seriously, but does not identify immediately perceptible qualitative capability differences as the basis for intuitive evaluation.

r003.rationale: It says benchmarks can saturate quickly and recommends continually building harder, more realistic tasks as the model develops.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about almost every day, because honestly, evaluation is the thing that breaks first when the paradigm shifts.

When the field moved from chat models to agents, most of our existing benchmarks became close to meaningless almost overnight. Not wrong, exactly, but they stopped measuring the thing we actually cared about. A benchmark like MMLU tells you whether a model knows things. It tells you nothing about whether the model can hold a goal over forty steps, recover when a tool call fails, or notice that it's been going down the wrong path for ten minutes. Those are the capabilities that matter in an agent setting, and the old static evals are basically blind to them.

So the first thing I'd say is: during a paradigm change, you have to be very honest with yourself about which of your metrics are still load-bearing. There's a strong temptation to keep optimizing the numbers you already have, because they're comparable across time and they look good in a report. But if the number is no longer connected to the capability you're trying to build, you're just training the model to be good at the exam.

The second thing is that in an agent paradigm, I think evaluation has to become much more environment-based and much less dataset-based. You can't capture agentic behavior in a question-answer pair. You need real environments: a codebase with actual tests, a browser, a file system, a sandbox where mistakes have consequences. We spent a lot of effort building those internally, and I'd argue the quality of your environments ends up being almost as important as the quality of your training data. If the environment is too easy or too artificial, the model learns to exploit it rather than to solve the underlying task.

Third, and this is the uncomfortable part, during a transition you have to accept that a lot of your evaluation will be qualitative for a while. Early on, we would just sit and watch trajectories. Read the whole trace, step by step. Where did it get confused? Did it hallucinate a tool output? Did it give up too early, or keep trying something that clearly wasn't working? That kind of reading is slow and doesn't scale, but it's how you discover what the new failure modes actually are. The quantitative benchmark comes after you understand the failure mode, not before.

And then there's a structural problem, which is that agent evals are expensive and noisy. A single run can take many steps, costs real compute, and the variance between runs is high. So you need to run things many times to get a signal, and that makes iteration slow. We had to think carefully about which evaluations go in the fast inner loop and which are the slow, expensive ones you only run on serious candidates.

One more thing I'd add. During a paradigm change, your eval should be slightly ahead of your model. If the model is passing everything, the eval has stopped being informative. I'd rather have a benchmark where we score thirty percent and the failures are interesting than one where we score ninety-five and we've stopped learning anything. The purpose of evaluation isn't to produce a nice number. It's to tell you what to build next.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluation challenges during a paradigm shift, but does not state that intuition can evaluate progress only during a brief window or that this depends on the development direction being right.

r002.rationale: It recommends reading trajectories to discover new failure modes, but does not identify immediately perceptible qualitative differences in capability as the basis for intuitive evaluation.

r003.rationale: It says quantitative benchmarks should follow understanding failure modes and distinguishes fast from expensive evaluations, but does not state that evaluations need to become increasingly refined as development moves beyond the initial phase.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is whether our evaluations are still measuring the capability we care about. When we move from a model that answers questions to an agent that takes actions, a correct final answer is only part of the picture. We also need to know whether it can plan, use feedback, recover from mistakes, and recognize when it needs help.

I would keep some stable evaluations so we can track progress, but add tasks that test this new way of working. Give the agent a goal and an environment, then look at both the outcome and the process: Did it actually finish? How much human intervention did it need? What did it cost in time and resources? If something went wrong, could it recover?

During a paradigm change, I would also spend more time examining individual failures. An aggregate score can hide very different problems. The important thing is to build a feedback loop where those failures help us improve the evaluation itself. Otherwise, we risk getting better at yesterday’s benchmark while missing what matters for the next generation of agents.

r001.rationale: The response does not describe a brief window for intuitive evaluation or condition it on developing in the right direction.

r002.rationale: It contrasts question-answering models with agents that act, but does not say that immediately perceptible qualitative differences ground intuitive evaluation.

r003.rationale: It recommends adding tasks and using failures to improve evaluations, but does not state that increasingly refined evaluations become necessary as development moves beyond an initial phase.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is whether our evaluations still measure the capability we actually care about. When a model moves from answering questions to acting as an agent, a correct final answer is only part of the picture. We also need to understand how it plans, uses tools, responds to feedback, and recovers when something goes wrong.

So I would keep some existing evaluations for continuity, but introduce tasks that require a complete workflow, with clear success criteria. Then I’d look closely at the failures. Did the model misunderstand the goal? Did it choose the wrong action? Or did it recognize a mistake but fail to recover? Those distinctions are much more useful than a single aggregate score.

During a paradigm change, the evaluation itself has to evolve. The important thing is to avoid confusing improvement on a familiar benchmark with improvement in the capability we’re trying to build.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention a brief window for intuition to assess progress or condition that judgment on development moving in the right direction.

r002.rationale: It describes agent behaviors to evaluate, but does not identify immediately perceptible qualitative differences as the basis for intuitive evaluation.

r003.rationale: It says evaluation should evolve during a paradigm change, but does not state that evaluations need to become increasingly refined after the initial phase.
